fried/crispy poha.note: Deep fried version, much higher fat

fun_facts: Poha absorbs less oil during cooking than rice, making it naturally lighter.
A plate of poha has roughly the same calories as 1.5 slices of bread.
The iron content in poha is surprisingly high because of the flattening process.
common_mistakes: People underestimate because it looks light and fluffy, but oil and peanuts add up.
visual_references: 1 katori = roughly a cricket ball volume = ~180 cal

fried idli / idli fry.note: Pan-fried with masala, nearly doubles calories

ghee podi idli.note: Ghee + gunpowder spice mix adds significant fat

fun_facts: A plain idli is one of the lowest calorie Indian breakfast items at just 52 calories each.
Idli batter fermentation creates probiotics that aid digestion.
The real calorie trap isn't the idli — it's the ghee and chutneys.
common_mistakes: People forget to count the accompaniments. 4 idli + sambar + chutney is ~350 cal, not 200.
visual_references: 1 idli = roughly the size of a hockey puck = ~52 cal

mysore masala dosa.note: Red chutney spread + potato + extra oil

set dosa.note: Smaller, thicker, less oil per piece

fun_facts: A restaurant masala dosa can have 350-400 calories — nearly as much as a McDonald's burger.
The difference between a home dosa and restaurant dosa can be 100+ calories purely from oil.
Rava dosa uses more oil to get crispy, despite seeming 'lighter'.
common_mistakes: Masala dosa is the classic underestimate. People think ~200 cal when it's closer to 350-400 with accompaniments.
visual_references: 1 regular dosa = roughly the area of a dinner plate = ~190 cal plain

rumali roti.note: Paper thin, lower cal per piece

fun_facts: The size of roti varies hugely — a dhaba roti can be 2x the calories of a home roti.
Adding ghee to each roti adds up fast: 3 rotis with ghee = extra 100+ calories vs dry.
Phulka (puffed roti) and chapati are the same thing — phulka just puffs on direct flame.
common_mistakes: People count rotis but forget the ghee. 3 rotis 'with a little ghee' can be 400+ cal.
visual_references: 1 medium roti = roughly the size of a standard plate rim = ~100 cal

fun_facts: A fist-sized portion of cooked rice is roughly 130 calories.
Most people eat 1.5-2 fists of rice without realizing it — that's 200-260 cal before any curry.
Brown rice has only 10-15% fewer calories than white rice — the real difference is fiber.
common_mistakes: The biggest rice mistake is portion blindness. People pour rice without measuring and often eat 300g+ thinking it was 'one serving'.
visual_references: 1 closed fist = ~100g cooked rice = ~130 cal

dal makhani.note: Butter + cream makes it very rich — 200+ cal per bowl

fun_facts: Plain boiled dal is very low calorie and high protein — one of the best Indian diet foods.
Dal makhani at a restaurant can have 2-3x the calories of home-cooked tadka dal.
The tadka (tempering) alone can add 50-80 calories to a bowl of dal.
common_mistakes: Dal makhani is the classic trap. It sounds healthy ('it's just dal') but restaurant versions are loaded with butter and cream.
visual_references: 1 katori of dal = roughly a tennis ball volume = ~110 cal for tadka dal

fun_facts: A restaurant butter chicken with 2 naans can easily be 900-1000 calories for one meal.
The 'butter' in butter chicken is real — a restaurant portion can have 3-4 tablespoons of butter.
Switching from butter chicken to tandoori chicken saves about 150-200 calories per serving.
common_mistakes: People guess ~300 cal for a restaurant serving when it's closer to 400-500 for the gravy alone.
visual_references: 1 restaurant bowl = roughly 250ml = ~375 cal

restaurant style.note: Heavy on cream and cashew paste

fun_facts: Paneer itself is 265 cal per 100g — it's one of the most calorie-dense vegetarian proteins.
A restaurant paneer butter masala can match a butter chicken in calories.
People assume vegetarian = lighter, but paneer curries are often MORE calorie-dense than chicken curries.
common_mistakes: The 'vegetarian is lighter' fallacy. Paneer butter masala is often 450-550 cal per serving.
visual_references: 6 cubes of paneer (100g) = roughly 265 cal before any gravy

fun_facts: A Swiggy single-serve biryani is often 700-800 calories — nearly half a day's intake.
The ghee layered between rice layers is what makes biryani calorie-dense vs plain rice + chicken.
Hyderabadi biryani tends to be richer than Lucknowi because of the dum cooking with more fat.
common_mistakes: Biryani is the most commonly underestimated Indian dish. People guess 400 when a Swiggy portion is 700-800.
visual_references: A standard delivery biryani container = ~400-450g = 700-800 cal

fun_facts: 2 regular samosas = about 500 calories, roughly the same as a full meal.
The outer pastry shell absorbs a LOT of oil during frying — that's where most calories hide.
A baked samosa has about 30% fewer calories than a fried one.
common_mistakes: 'It's just a snack' — but 2 samosas with chutney = 550+ cal.
visual_references: 1 regular samosa = roughly the size of your palm = ~250 cal

with butter on top.note: The classic Punjabi finish — extra 50 cal

fun_facts: 2 aloo parathas with butter and curd = 750-800 calories. That's a full meal's worth at breakfast.
A restaurant paratha uses 2-3x more ghee/oil than a home-cooked one.
The stuffing matters less than you think — the real calories are in the dough layers and cooking fat.
common_mistakes: People focus on the stuffing (aloo vs gobhi) but ignore the ghee/butter. A 'light' gobhi paratha with extra butter = same as aloo.
visual_references: 1 aloo paratha = roughly a dinner plate diameter = ~310 cal

fun_facts: One butter naan has about 320 calories — nearly as much as a full plate of rice.
Most people eat 2-3 naans with a curry, adding 600-900 calories just from bread.
Naan uses maida (refined flour), yogurt, and oil in the dough — it's richer than roti by default.
common_mistakes: Naan vs roti: people think they're similar, but one naan = 2.5 to 3 rotis in calories.
visual_references: 1 naan = roughly the size of a large hand spread = ~260 cal plain

chole bhature combo.note: Bhatura alone is 300+ cal. Full combo = 600-700

fun_facts: Chole alone is actually quite healthy — high protein, high fiber. The problem is what you eat it WITH.
A chole bhature plate at a dhaba can be 700-800 calories total.
Chickpeas are one of the best plant protein sources at ~19g protein per 100g dry.
common_mistakes: Chole bhature: people think of it as one dish but it's really 250 cal (chole) + 350 cal (bhatura) + oil.
visual_references: 1 katori chole = tennis ball volume = ~180 cal

fun_facts: Street-side pav bhaji uses an obscene amount of butter — some vendors use a quarter block per plate.
The pav (bread) alone is ~150 cal per piece. Most plates come with 2-3 pavs.
The bhaji is mostly vegetables and is the healthier part — it's the butter and pav that add up.
common_mistakes: 'It's just vegetables and bread' — a street pav bhaji plate can be 600-700 calories.
visual_references: 1 street plate = ~550-650 cal with standard 2 pav

standard.note: Fried vada in pav with chutneys

fun_facts: A vada pav has about the same calories as a McDonald's McAloo Tikki burger.
It's called the 'Indian burger' for good reason — similar calorie density too.
The deep-fried vada absorbs a lot of oil. That's where 40% of the calories come from.
common_mistakes: Seems like a small snack, but at 290 cal each, 2 vada pavs = a full meal's calories.
visual_references: 1 vada pav = roughly the size of a tennis ball in a bun = ~290 cal

fun_facts: Upma and poha have very similar calories — upma just feels heavier because semolina is denser.
The oil used for tempering can account for 25-30% of upma's total calories.
common_mistakes: Upma seems lighter than poha but it's about the same. The semolina + oil tempering is calorie-comparable.
visual_references: 1 plate upma = roughly the same as 1 plate poha = ~300 cal

fun_facts: Rajma is one of the best plant protein sources — 24g protein per 100g dry beans.
Rajma chawal is a complete protein meal — the rice and beans together provide all essential amino acids.
A full rajma chawal plate (bowl of rajma + plate of rice) = about 550-650 calories.
common_mistakes: People estimate rajma and rice separately and still get it wrong. The combo is 550-650 cal.
visual_references: 1 katori rajma = tennis ball = ~165 cal; add 1 plate rice = 425 total

with milk + 2 tsp sugar.note: Extra sugar adds ~20 cal per tsp

fun_facts: 3-4 cups of regular chai per day = 200-350 extra calories that most people don't count.
The sugar in chai is the hidden calorie bomb. Each teaspoon adds ~20 calories.
A cutting chai from a tapri is one of the lowest-calorie warm beverages at just 30 cal.
common_mistakes: Nobody counts chai calories. 4 cups/day with 2 tsp sugar each = 300+ invisible calories.
visual_references: 1 regular cup = ~55 cal; cutting chai = ~30 cal

fun_facts: Each gulab jamun is a calorie triple threat: deep fried dough + soaked in sugar syrup + made from khoya (reduced milk).
2 gulab jamuns = 260 calories, roughly the same as a full bowl of dal chawal.
The sugar syrup alone accounts for about 40% of the calories.
common_mistakes: They're small so people eat 3-4. That's 400-500 calories of pure sugar and fat.
visual_references: 1 gulab jamun = roughly the size of a golf ball = ~130 cal

standard.note: Deep fried and sugar syrup soaked

fun_facts: Jalebi is one of the most calorie-dense Indian sweets at 380 cal per 100g.
A small plate of jalebi with rabri can be 500+ calories — basically a full meal.
The deep frying + sugar syrup soak is a calorie double hit.
common_mistakes: They look light and airy, but each jalebi ring is soaked in sugar syrup and fried. 3 pieces = 300+ cal.
visual_references: 1 jalebi ring = ~115 cal; a standard plate = ~300 cal

fun_facts: Each tiny pani puri is about 40 calories. A standard serving of 6 = 240 calories.
The puri shell is deep fried — that's where most calories hide, not the water filling.
Nobody stops at 6. A typical street-side session of 10-12 puris = 400-500 calories.
common_mistakes: 'It's just water and a tiny shell' — but 10 puris = 400 cal, mainly from the fried shells.
visual_references: 1 pani puri = ping pong ball size = ~40 cal each

fun_facts: A single Maggi pack is 310 calories — not terrible for a snack, but most people cook two packs.
60% of Maggi's calories come from the noodle block (fried before packaging), not the masala.
Hostel Maggi with butter, cheese, and egg can hit 500+ calories easily.
common_mistakes: Double pack Maggi is 620 cal — that's a full meal but most people eat it AS a snack on top of meals.
visual_references: 1 pack cooked = roughly a large bowl = ~310 cal

fun_facts: Egg bhurji is one of the best protein-to-calorie ratios in Indian street food.
2-egg bhurji with light oil = 200 cal with 14g protein. Hard to beat that.
The street-side anda pav version doubles the calories because of the buttered pav.
common_mistakes: The bhurji itself is fine. It's the 2 buttered pavs that turn a 200-cal snack into 500 cal.
visual_references: 2-egg bhurji = roughly half a plate = ~200 cal

fun_facts: A Punjabi tall glass sweet lassi = 280 cal. That's a liquid meal people drink alongside their actual meal.
Switching from sweet to salted lassi saves 100+ calories per glass.
Mango lassi at restaurants often uses sugar AND mango pulp — double sweetness, 200+ cal.
common_mistakes: Beverages don't register as 'food' mentally. A tall lassi adds 280 cal to a meal without feeling like it.
visual_references: 1 regular glass = ~175 cal sweet; ~70 cal salted

fun_facts: Aloo gobi is one of the lighter curries — if it's not deep-fried first.
The difference between a home-cooked and restaurant aloo gobi can be 50-70% more calories due to oil.
Cauliflower is only 25 cal/100g. The potato and oil are doing all the calorie work.
common_mistakes: Restaurant versions often deep-fry the cauliflower first, which almost doubles the calories vs. home-cooked.
visual_references: 1 katori = ~145 cal homemade — a lighter curry option

fun_facts: The spinach (palak) in palak paneer is practically zero calories. It's the paneer and cream doing the heavy lifting.
100g of paneer = 265 calories. A standard portion of palak paneer has about 100-150g of paneer in it.
Switching to tofu instead of paneer saves about 40% calories.
common_mistakes: 'Green = healthy' — but the paneer and cream make this a 350+ cal dish per restaurant bowl.
visual_references: 1 katori = ~210 cal; restaurant bowl = ~350 cal

fun_facts: A medium banana is ~105 cal. It's one of the easiest food items to remember for calibration.
Banana is the gold standard reference food: if you can estimate a banana, you can estimate most fruits.
A banana shake with full cream milk and sugar = 250-300 cal. The banana is the least of it.
common_mistakes: People often think bananas are higher calorie than they are. A medium banana = just 105 cal.
visual_references: 1 medium banana = ~105 cal — use this as your mental calibration anchor
